# `generator-shortcuts` answer

The strongest plausible shortcut is: **use Manhattan distance, but when multiple seeds are tied, choose the lower seed color instead of the seed that appears first in row-major reading order**. This is a natural rival because all three canonical pairs happen to make the lower-color decision agree with the intended reading-order decision, so it fits 3/3 canonical demonstrations exactly. A second complete canonical shortcut is “ignore every seed after the first two,” because every canonical input has only two seeds.

A generated counterexample is retained at `checks/shortcut-witness/witness.json` (generator SHA-256 `e2271d4ce81f37366d64781ce5f29f087e748e3211cd869f1e67181c5d7bb44b`, seed `314159`, sample index `0`, medium):

```json
[
  [8,8,8,8,8,8,8],
  [8,0,0,0,0,0,8],
  [8,0,0,0,0,3,8],
  [8,0,0,0,1,0,8],
  [8,0,0,0,0,0,8],
  [8,8,8,8,8,8,8]
]
```

The selected Racket rule returns:

```json
[
  [8,8,8,8,8,8,8],
  [8,3,3,3,3,3,8],
  [8,3,3,3,3,3,8],
  [8,1,1,1,1,3,8],
  [8,1,1,1,1,3,8],
  [8,8,8,8,8,8,8]
]
```

The lower-color shortcut instead returns:

```json
[
  [8,8,8,8,8,8,8],
  [8,1,1,1,1,3,8],
  [8,1,1,1,1,3,8],
  [8,1,1,1,1,1,8],
  [8,1,1,1,1,1,8],
  [8,8,8,8,8,8,8]
]
```

They disagree at ten cells: `(1,1)` through `(1,4)`, `(2,1)` through `(2,4)`, `(3,5)`, and `(4,5)`. I generated the input with the supported `arcpuzzles generate` command, applied the selected Racket rule with `arcpuzzles apply`, and retained the hash-bound output at `checks/shortcut-witness/racket.json`; the independent Python rival probe produced the alternative output.

Yes, the repaired generator deliberately emits such cases. Every default `sample_index % 3 == 0` is a `tie_order` role: it constructs at least one Manhattan tie and assigns colors in descending order to row-major-sorted seeds, forcing the reading-order and lower-color rules to disagree. The other two schedule slots separately force a consequential third seed and a Manhattan-versus-Euclidean disagreement.
